body:
The Writing System of the Harappans

The Harappans used a distinctive system of signs known as the Indus script or Harappan script. Its surviving inscriptions form an important part of the material culture of the Mature Harappan period, approximately 2600–1900 BCE.

The script is especially well known from seals, but it was not confined to them. Signs have been found on several different kinds of objects, demonstrating that writing or inscription-making was practised in more than one setting.

Where Indus Signs Have Been Found

  • Stone seals: Usually containing a short sequence of signs above or near an engraved motif.
  • Copper and terracotta tablets: Small objects bearing signs, figures or both.
  • Pottery: Signs occurring on vessels, including jar rims.
  • Other objects: Examples include copper tools, jewellery and bone rods.
  • Dholavira: A remarkable group of large signs associated with a gateway rather than a small portable object.

The variety of objects suggests that the signs served purposes that extended beyond decorating seals. Their actual meanings, however, remain unknown.

Important Characteristics of the Script

A Large Inventory of Signs

NCERT describes the script as having approximately 375–400 signs. The exact number depends partly on how distinct signs and their variations are classified.

This inventory is substantially larger than that of a simple alphabet in which each sign ordinarily represents a single vowel or consonant. Consequently, the script should not be described as an established alphabet comparable to modern English writing.

Its exact linguistic structure remains uncertain. Some scholars have proposed that signs represented words, syllables or combinations of these, but no interpretation has achieved general acceptance.

Short Inscriptions

Most surviving Indus inscriptions are extremely short, often containing only a few signs. The standard NCERT account reports a longest inscription of approximately 26 signs in the corpus it describes.

Short inscriptions are difficult to interpret because they provide little context. A brief sequence might identify an individual, a commodity, a group or something else, but these possibilities cannot be established through translation.

Probable Direction of Writing

The predominant direction of writing on many Indus seals appears to have been from right to left.

One supporting observation is that signs on some inscriptions are more widely spaced towards the right and crowded together towards the left. This suggests that an engraver may have started on the right and had progressively less space while moving leftward.

This is a general characteristic inferred from the evidence. It should not be taken to mean that every surviving inscription necessarily follows exactly the same arrangement.

The Dholavira Signboard

Dholavira, on Khadir Bet in the Kutch region of Gujarat, provides one of the most striking examples of large-scale Harappan writing.

Excavations revealed 10 large Harappan signs associated with the northern gateway of the Castle area. The characters were made using white gypsum and were probably inlaid into a wooden board. The wooden material has decomposed, leaving the surviving signs.

Unlike the small inscriptions commonly seen on seals, these comparatively large characters were probably intended to be visible from a distance.

The signboard demonstrates that Harappan signs were sometimes used in architectural settings. Its inscription has not been securely translated, so it cannot be stated as a fact that the signs recorded the city's name, a ruler's title or any particular message.

Why the Script Remains Undeciphered

A script is deciphered when its signs and their relationships can be interpreted sufficiently reliably to read the written content. Merely recognising or counting its signs is not the same as deciphering their meaning.

Researchers have identified recurring signs, patterns and probable writing conventions. Nevertheless, the language represented by the inscriptions has not been securely established.

Two major difficulties are the brevity of surviving inscriptions and the absence of an accepted bilingual text that provides the same message in Indus signs and a known language.

As of the content cutoff of 17 November 2026, no decipherment of the Indus script has gained general scholarly acceptance. The Government of India's Ministry of Culture explicitly stated that the script had not been successfully deciphered in its Rajya Sabha answer dated 13 March 2025. Subsequent reporting in 2026 continued to describe the script as undeciphered.

Accordingly, claims that a particular Indus inscription definitively records Sanskrit, a Dravidian language, a specific deity, a royal title or a named individual should not be treated as established facts.

Recognising signs is not the same as reading them. The script's appearance, approximate sign inventory and probable writing direction can be studied even though its linguistic content remains unresolved.

Prelims focus

  • Status: Indus script remains undeciphered at the 17 November 2026 cutoff.
  • Signs: Approximately 375–400 in the standard NCERT account.
  • Direction: Predominantly right to left.
  • Inscriptions: Usually short; approximately 26 signs in the longest inscription described by NCERT.
  • Dholavira: 10 large gypsum signs associated with the northern gateway.
  • Trap: The language and exact meaning of Indus inscriptions have not been established.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, Section 7.2, An Enigmatic Script, printed p. 15; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class VI, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, printed p. 39; Archaeological Survey of India, Rajkot Circle, Dholavira: A Harappan City, Signboard section, reproduced in UNESCO World Heritage Centre document 185385; Government of India, Ministry of Culture, Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 1623, Harappan Script, answered 13 March 2025; Live Science, Will the Indus Valley Script Ever Be Deciphered?, 15 March 2026. Online sources consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: The Indus Script: Signs, Writing Direction and the Problem of Decipherment

body:
Metrology in the Harappan Civilisation

Metrology is the study and practice of measurement. In the Harappan context, it includes the use of standard weights, regular proportions and consistent dimensions in the manufacture of objects and construction of buildings.

Harappan settlements were spread over a large geographical region, yet certain artefacts display remarkable uniformity. Similar weights, seals and brick proportions occur at different settlements.

This consistency indicates that Harappan craftspeople used shared practical standards. Such standards would have been valuable for exchanging goods, producing objects and constructing buildings.

The Harappan System of Weights

Harappan weights were commonly made from chert, a hard stone. Many were carefully shaped into small cubes.

The weights were generally unmarked. Their values depended on their measured masses rather than written numerical labels on their surfaces.

Archaeologists have identified a regulated series of weight values. This is important because the objects were not simply stones chosen at random for weighing.

Binary Progression in Smaller Denominations

In the standard textbook description, smaller weight denominations followed a binary progression, involving repeated doubling.

Examples of the relative denominations are:

\(1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 32\)

Each successive value in this sequence is twice the preceding value. For example, 2 units are twice 1 unit, while 8 units are twice 4 units.

These are relative weight values, not measurements in modern grams. They illustrate the numerical relationships used to organise a set of standard weights.

Decimal Relationships in Higher Denominations

The larger weights also displayed decimal relationships, involving multiples based on 10.

Thus, the standard textbook account describes a system containing binary relationships in smaller denominations and decimal relationships among larger denominations.

The existence of these patterns demonstrates numerical regularity in measurement. It does not establish the complete numeral system used by the Harappans in their undeciphered writing.

Uses of Standard Weights

The smaller weights were probably useful for weighing valuable goods, including beads and jewellery materials. Metal scale-pans have also been discovered.

A standard weight system allowed quantities to be compared more consistently between people and settlements. This was especially useful where goods were exchanged or stored.

However, a standard weight is not the same as a coin. Harappan stone weights should not be described as a monetary currency.

Geometry in Brick Construction

Harappan builders used regularly proportioned bricks, both sun-dried and baked. An important standard was the relationship between a brick's length, breadth and height.

The common proportion can be expressed as:

\(\text{Length}:\text{Breadth}:\text{Height}=4:2:1\)

This means that, in the standard proportion, the length is 4 times the height and the breadth is 2 times the height.

For example, a brick with a height of 1 relative unit would have a breadth of 2 relative units and a length of 4 relative units.

The significance lies in the ratio, not in assuming that every Harappan brick had exactly the same physical dimensions. Bricks of different sizes could still follow the same proportional rule.

Geometry in Urban Layouts

Harappan urban planning also demonstrates practical knowledge of straight lines, rectangular forms and right angles.

At Mohenjodaro, many streets followed an approximately grid-like arrangement, with roads intersecting at or near right angles. This layout helped organise buildings and the routes used by people and drainage channels.

The use of a right angle is associated with a geometric relationship of 90 degrees. Recognising and reproducing right angles is useful when laying out rectangular streets, courtyards, rooms and tanks.

Standardised proportions also made construction more predictable. Builders working with bricks of regular shapes could produce more consistent walls and align structural elements.

These achievements demonstrate practical geometrical understanding. They do not prove that Harappan builders possessed any particular later mathematical theorem or written mathematical treatise.

Measurement and Urban Organisation

The combination of standard weights and regular construction proportions suggests that measurement was important in several areas of Harappan life.

  • Exchange: Standard weights allowed more consistent comparison of quantities.
  • Craft production: Regular shapes and dimensions supported the manufacture of comparable objects.
  • Construction: Standard brick proportions helped builders create regular structures.
  • Town planning: Straight streets, right angles and measured spaces supported organised urban layouts.

These shared standards indicate coordination across Harappan settlements. They do not, on their own, establish the precise political institutions responsible for maintaining them.

Prelims focus

  • Common weight material: Chert.
  • Common weight shape: Cubical, generally without markings.
  • Smaller denominations: Binary progression such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32.
  • Larger denominations: Decimal relationships.
  • Brick proportion: Length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
  • Trap: Standard weights are not evidence of a system of coinage.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, Sections 3.1, 7.3 and 8, printed pp. 6–7 and 15–16; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class VI, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, printed pp. 33–36; Harappa Archaeological Research Project, Weights, Harappa, Around the Indus in 90 Slides, consulted 17 November 2026.]
